hints: Start on the far left where the receptor cells touch the neurone and trace the impulse towards the right - the first fine branches that collect the signal have a special name.
Follow the long myelinated fibre on the left of the cell body (B) and on the right of the cell body (D) - think about which part carries the impulse towards the cell body in a sensory neurone.
Look at the swollen part labelled C containing the nucleus - this is the metabolic centre of the neurone.
Compare the two long myelinated regions - B is the dendron side leading into the cell body, D is the axon side leading away toward the CNS.
walkthrough:
Picture the route of the impulse**
In this sensory neurone the signal starts in the receptor cells on the left and travels to the right toward the spinal cord or brain. The very fine branching fibres labelled A make direct contact with the receptors to pick up the receptor potential.

Name the receiving branches and the first fibre**
Those fine branches are dendrites. They join to form the longer myelinated fibre labelled B that carries the impulse toward the cell body. In a sensory neurone this is called the dendron, also accepted as the sensory axon.

Identify the nucleus-containing swelling**
Label C points to the bulge containing the nucleus and most cytoplasm. That is the cell body, also called the soma or centron. It sits to one side in a sensory neurone and maintains the cell.

Name the output fibre**
After the cell body the impulse continues along the second long myelinated fibre labelled D toward the nerve endings. That is the axon.
Final answer: A - dendrite(s); B - dendron / sensory axon; C - cell body / soma / centron; D - axon.

hints: Think about what myelin is made of - layers of Schwann cell membrane rich in lipid - and what that means for movement of $Na^+$ and $K^+$ ions across the axon membrane underneath it.
If ions cannot move where myelin covers the axon, where along the axon can an action potential still be regenerated, and how does that change the way the impulse travels?
walkthrough:
Why myelin blocks ion flow**
Myelin is many layers of lipid-rich membrane. It acts as an electrical insulator, so $Na^+$ and $K^+$ cannot cross the axon membrane where it is covered and no action potential can form there.

How the impulse jumps**
Gaps in the myelin called nodes of Ranvier have exposed membrane with voltage-gated channels. Depolarisation and action potentials happen only at these nodes, and local circuits are set up between one node and the next. The impulse appears to jump from node to node, called saltatory conduction, which is much faster than travelling along the whole membrane.
Final answer: Myelin insulates the axon so depolarisation / action potentials occur only at nodes of Ranvier; impulses jump from node to node by saltatory conduction, increasing speed.

hints: Match each bar in Fig. 8.3 in order to each event in Fig. 8.2 - compare the height of the stimulus bar with the height of the membrane potential peak that follows it.
Look at the dashed line at $-50$ $mV$ in Fig. 8.2 - which small depolarisation fails to cross it and what happens, compared to the larger stimuli that do cross it?
walkthrough:
Separate sub-threshold from supra-threshold**
The first small bar in Fig. 8.3 produces only a small receptor potential that stays below about $-50$ $mV$ in Fig. 8.2, so no action potential follows. The next three larger stimuli all push the potential to threshold and each triggers a full spike to about $+40$ $mV$.

See that size does not grow with stimulus**
Although the three successful stimuli in Fig. 8.3 get progressively taller, the three action potentials in Fig. 8.2 are all identical in amplitude. Once threshold is reached the response is maximal and constant. That is the all-or-nothing law.

Final answer: Only a stimulus that depolarises the membrane to threshold (about $-50$ $mV$) triggers an action potential; all action potentials produced are the same size regardless of stimulus strength - all-or-nothing response.
